problem: The lead says 'a caller cannot push an impossible value into an object'. In Python this is too strong: the chapter's own exam trap 2 shows that t.__celsius = -300 from module level creates a new attribute and breaks the object. A student may read the lead as a guarantee that Python enforces.
fix: Say 'a caller who uses the public methods cannot push an impossible value into an object' and keep the convention-based caveat from Section 1.

problem: The examples 'a datetime, a pandas DataFrame' are loose. datetime is immutable and offers no setters, so it is not an accessor/mutator example; a DataFrame lets callers assign many attributes directly with little validation. Both weaken the point being made.
fix: Use examples that really validate or hide storage, such as decimal.Decimal (immutable, validated) and a small Account class with a balance setter, or drop the library list.

problem: 'The double underscore is called name mangling' confuses the trigger with the process. Name mangling is the renaming that Python performs; the double underscore prefix is what triggers it.
fix: Write: 'The leading double underscore triggers name mangling. Name mangling is the renaming Python performs.'

problem: 'Inside the class the source says __celsius; outside, name mangling makes it _Temperature__celsius' suggests the rename happens when code outside runs. The rename happens at compile time, in the class body, before anything runs.
fix: Write: 'The source inside the class says __celsius. Python rewrites that name to _Temperature__celsius at compile time, so from outside you must use t._Temperature__celsius.'

problem: Missing point: __init__ writes self.__celsius = 0 directly. This attribute is the mangled _Temperature__celsius, not the property celsius, so the validation check does not run at construction. A student may assume the setter runs when the object is created.
fix: Add one line: '__init__ assigns the private attribute directly, so the check does not run for the starting value; write self.celsius = 0 if you want the setter to validate it too.'

problem: Section 2 says 'The figure follows two calls on one object', but the figure is printed after Section 4, several screens later, so the pointer is misleading on a phone.
fix: Move the figure directly after Section 2, or say in Section 2: 'The figure at the end of Section 4 follows two calls on one object.'
